case_title: Arvind Kumar v. State of NCT, Delhi
accused_occupation: Police guard (posted as a guard at the police station)
accused_victim_relationship: Co-worker: both were police personnel at the same police station; alleged prior enmity (compromising-position motive) was not established
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged, set aside); IPC s.304A (finally established)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (two witnesses), ballistic expert reports, circumstantial evidence, res gestae statements under s.6 Evidence Act
confession: None; the alleged statement blaming the duty officer was held not to be a confession of guilt
mitigating_circumstances: Accidental firing; no intention to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death; no knowledge attributed
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 IPC; sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The victim, a police constable working as record keeper at a police station, was using the station's official telephone in the reporting room for five to seven minutes. The duty officer, a sub-inspector, told the victim to free the line because urgent calls might come in, but the victim continued the call. Around 5.55 pm the duty officer asked the accused, a guard posted at the station and carrying a semi-automatic fire carbine, to ask the victim to end the call. The accused entered the room, placed a hand on the victim's shoulder and asked the victim to end the call. The prosecution's initial account was that the victim playfully pushed the accused while holding the carbine. During the struggle the carbine became entangled in the chain attached to the accused's belt, and five rounds fired. Five bullets struck the victim in the neck and chest. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. An offence was first registered on the duty officer's statement. The victim's father complained to senior police officers, and the investigation was transferred to the Crime Branch, which alleged that the victim had seen the accused and the duty officer in a compromising position and that they had threatened to kill him. Ballistic reports recorded close-range firing. A later report stated that the carbine could be cocked by entanglement with a chain if the change lever was not at the safety position, and would then fire if the trigger was pressed. Eyewitness accounts described the entanglement and accidental firing. A witness said he heard the accused tell the duty officer that the accused's children would be ruined, and heard the duty officer's reply. Several other persons present did not support the prosecution.
offence_severity: Maximum two years imprisonment under s.304A as stated in the judgment; no minimum stated
physical_harm: Death from five gunshot wounds to the neck and chest
number_of_offences: 1 charged; 1 finally upheld (s.304A, a lesser offence)
premeditation_planning: Not found; the court held there was no intention to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death
motive: alleged: deceased had seen the accused and the duty officer in a compromising position; motive not established
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of PW-12 and PW-25 (accidental entanglement and firing); second and third ballistic expert opinions (chain entanglement can cock the carbine if change lever not at safety); fact of five bullet injuries
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses PW-12 and PW-25 were not declared hostile and their accounts support accidental firing; the motive testimony of PW-22 was disbelieved; accounts of PW-5 and PW-13 about the alleged statements did not inspire confidence
post_offence_conduct: Alleged statement blaming the duty officer immediately after the firing; court treated it as relevant conduct only if made, without accepting the witness version
custody_duration: About 8 years and 11 months before release on bail
bail_history: Released on bail by the Supreme Court by order dated 27 November 2017
trial_duration: offence: 28 December 1994; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 02.07.2010; Supreme Court: 17 July 2023
legal_representation: Appellant: S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Adv., Ms. Prerna Mehta, Adv. State: Jayant K. Sud, ASG, with other advocates for the respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered under s.304A; investigation transferred to Crime Branch; chargesheet filed under s.302; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Intentional-firing case was not put to the appellant in his s.313 CrPC statement
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life sentence. High Court: conviction confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal partly allowed; s.302 conviction set aside; convicted under s.304A
prosecution_argument: Ballistic and ocular evidence showed the accused knew that use of the SAF carbine may cause death
defence_argument: Accidental firing; no offence under s.80 IPC; alternatively s.304 Part II applies; circumstantial case fails once motive discarded
legal_principle_applied: Culpable homicide under s.299 IPC not established; gross negligence leading to death punishable under s.304A; s.6 Evidence Act res gestae relevance
sentencing_rationale: Maximum sentence for s.304A already undergone, so further detention not required
judicial_mitigating_factors: Accidental firing; no intention or knowledge that death was likely; over eight years already undergone
judicial_aggravating_factors: Gross negligence in failing to keep the change lever at safety while holding a sophisticated automatic weapon
